note.explanation: In the Brønsted–Lowry concept, an acid gives a proton and a base takes a proton. Water can do either, depending on what it reacts with.
examples: HCl gives a proton to H₂O, so HCl is the acid and H₂O is the base.
NH₃ takes a proton from H₂O, so NH₃ is the base and H₂O is the acid.
note.checkAnswer: Water is amphoteric because it can behave as both an acid and a base.
note.simple: An acid hands over H⁺. A base receives H⁺. Water can do either job.
note.checkQuestion: What is a substance called if it can behave as both an acid and a base?
note.title: Brønsted–Lowry Acids and Bases
steps: Find which substance donates H⁺: it is the acid.
Find which substance accepts H⁺: it is the base.
The acid left after donating H⁺ is its conjugate base.
The base formed after accepting H⁺ is its conjugate acid.
note.answer: An acid donates a proton; a base accepts a proton.

options: A substance that donates a proton

mcqs.stem: According to the Brønsted–Lowry concept, what is an acid?
rationales: Correct: a Brønsted–Lowry acid donates a proton.
Incorrect: a substance that accepts a proton is a Brønsted–Lowry base.
Incorrect: this describes a restricted water-based idea, not the Brønsted–Lowry definition.
Incorrect: accepting an electron is not the definition given in this section.

options: Donates a proton
Accepts a proton
Must contain a hydroxyl group
Must react only in water
mcqs.stem: Which statement best defines a Brønsted–Lowry base?
rationales: Incorrect: a proton donor is an acid.
Correct: a Brønsted–Lowry base accepts a proton.
Incorrect: a base need not contain a hydroxyl group.
Incorrect: a Brønsted–Lowry reaction may occur in the gas phase or in a solvent.

mcqs.stem: In HCl(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻, which substance donates a proton?
rationales: Correct: HCl donates H⁺ to water.
Incorrect: water accepts a proton in this reaction.
Incorrect: H₃O⁺ is formed after water accepts a proton.
Incorrect: Cl⁻ is formed when HCl donates its proton.

mcqs.stem: In NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ OH⁻ + NH₄⁺, which roles do NH₃ and H₂O play?
rationales: Incorrect: NH₃ accepts, rather than donates, a proton here.
Correct: NH₃ accepts a proton and H₂O donates it.
Incorrect: NH₃ accepts a proton, so it is acting as a base.
Incorrect: a proton is transferred from H₂O to NH₃.

mcqs.stem: What does amphoteric mean in this section?
rationales: Correct: an amphoteric compound can behave as both an acid and a base.
Incorrect: amphoteric compounds can act as acids in suitable reactions.
Incorrect: the section defines amphoteric behaviour in terms of acid and base action, not electrons.
Incorrect: an amphoteric compound can also behave as a base.

mcqs.stem: In HCl + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻, which product is the conjugate base of HCl?
rationales: Correct: Cl⁻ is what remains after HCl donates a proton.
Incorrect: HCl is the acid that donates the proton.
Incorrect: H₂O accepts a proton in the forward reaction.
Incorrect: H₃O⁺ is the conjugate acid formed from H₂O.

rationales: Correct: NH₄⁺ is formed when NH₃ accepts a proton.
Incorrect: OH⁻ is the conjugate base formed when H₂O donates a proton.
Incorrect: NH₃ is the base before accepting a proton.

mcqs.stem: What makes a reaction an acid–base reaction according to Brønsted–Lowry?
rationales: Incorrect: the section says the reaction may occur in the gas phase or in a solvent.
Correct: the reaction involves proton transfer from a proton donor to its acceptor.
Incorrect: the definition is based on proton donation, not on an acid releasing a hydroxyl group.
Incorrect: the section defines the reaction by proton transfer, not by the formation of salt and water.

written.text: Give two examples of Brønsted–Lowry bases which are not bases by Arrhenius definition.
written.finalAnswer: NH₃ and CN⁻ are two examples.

written.text:
Q7.2. In the presence of a drop of an acid, water is known to ionize as follows:

H₂O (l) ⇌ H⁺ (aq) + OH⁻ (aq)

In your opinion, which name will be suitable for water: an acid, a base or both?
written.finalAnswer: Both; water is amphoteric because it can behave as an acid and as a base.

rubric.why: The question asks whether water is an acid, a base, or both.
rubric.how: State that water can be both an acid and a base.

rubric.why: The section names a substance that can act as both an acid and a base amphoteric.
A substance behaves as an acid when it donates a proton.
rubric.how: Explain that water can donate H⁺.

rubric.why: A substance behaves as a base when it accepts a proton.
rubric.how: Explain that water can accept H⁺.

modelAnswer: Water can act as an acid by donating a proton (H⁺).
Water can act as a base by accepting a proton (H⁺).
Therefore, water can behave as both an acid and a base.
Water is called an amphoteric compound.

written.text: Q7.3. Why does Na₂CO₃ behave like a base in water?
written.finalAnswer: Na₂CO₃ behaves like a base in water because it yields OH⁻ in water, although it contains no hydroxyl group to ionize.

rubric.why: The section identifies the production of OH⁻ in water as the observed basic behaviour.
rubric.description: State what Na₂CO₃ yields in water.
rubric.how: Say that it yields OH⁻ in water.

rubric.why: This point explains why Na₂CO₃ is an example of a base that the simple Arrhenius description does not readily account for.

rubric.how: State that Na₂CO₃ has no hydroxyl group to ionize in water.

modelAnswer: Na₂CO₃ does not contain a hydroxyl group that will get ionized by water.
However, it behaves as a base and yields OH⁻ in water.

written.text: Q7.2. Compare Arrhenius and Brønsted – Lowry concepts of acids and bases.
written.finalAnswer: Arrhenius concept requires water, whereas Brønsted–Lowry defines an acid as a proton donor and a base as a proton acceptor; proton transfer can occur in a gas phase or in any solvent.

rubric.why: The section points out that the Arrhenius concept requires water to be present.
rubric.description: State the water requirement of the Arrhenius concept.
rubric.how: Explain that the Arrhenius definitions require water as the solvent.

rubric.why: Proton donation is the Brønsted–Lowry definition of an acid.
rubric.how: State that an acid donates a proton.

rubric.why: Proton acceptance is the Brønsted–Lowry definition of a base.
rubric.how: State that a base accepts a proton.

rubric.why: Brønsted–Lowry proton transfer is not restricted to water.
rubric.description: State the broader scope of the Brønsted–Lowry concept.
rubric.how: Mention that the reaction may occur in the gas phase or in the presence of any solvent.

modelAnswer: Arrhenius definitions require water to be present as a solvent for a compound to behave as an acid or a base.
According to Brønsted–Lowry, an acid is a substance that donates a proton.
A base is a substance that accepts a proton.
A proton-transfer reaction may take place in the gas phase or in the presence of any solvent.

written.text: Q7.6. Differentiate between an acid and its conjugate base.
written.finalAnswer: An acid donates a proton; its conjugate base is the species left after that proton is donated and can accept a proton in the reverse reaction.

rubric.why: Proton donation distinguishes an acid in this concept.
rubric.how: State that an acid donates a proton.

rubric.why: The conjugate base is related to the acid after the acid loses a proton.
rubric.description: Describe how the conjugate base is formed.
rubric.how: Say that it is formed when the acid donates a proton.

rubric.why: The conjugate base can accept a proton in the reverse reaction.
rubric.how: Explain that it can accept a proton.

rubric.why: The proton difference makes the relationship between an acid and its conjugate base clear.
rubric.how: Explain that the conjugate base has one fewer proton than its acid.

modelAnswer: An acid is a substance that donates a proton.
The species left after the acid donates a proton is its conjugate base.
The conjugate base can accept a proton in the reverse reaction.
An acid and its conjugate base differ by one proton.

examTips: This section can appear as a short-answer question asking you to define a Brønsted–Lowry acid or base, or to identify them in a reaction.
For reaction questions, follow the H⁺: the donor is the acid and the acceptor is the base. Then identify the conjugate acid and conjugate base if asked.
For comparison questions, earn marks by stating both proton definitions and explaining that Brønsted–Lowry reactions do not require water.
For a question about water, use the term amphoteric and explain that water can donate or accept a proton.

steps.why: The reaction shows HCl and H₂O as the reactants and the products formed after proton transfer.
HCl gives H⁺ to water, so it is the proton donor and therefore the acid.
H₂O receives H⁺ from HCl, so it is the proton acceptor and therefore the base.
After HCl donates H⁺, Cl⁻ remains as its conjugate base; after H₂O accepts H⁺, H₃O⁺ is its conjugate acid.
steps.text: H₃O⁺ is the conjugate acid and Cl⁻ is the conjugate base.

example.question: For HCl(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻, identify the acid, base, conjugate acid and conjugate base.
example.answer: HCl is the acid, H₂O is the base, H₃O⁺ is the conjugate acid and Cl⁻ is the conjugate base.

explain.title: The Brønsted–Lowry idea
explain.body: The section gives these definitions: “An acid is a substance that donates a proton.” and “A base is a substance that accepts a proton.” A proton is H⁺. Look for which substance gives H⁺ and which one receives it.

explain.title: How this differs from Arrhenius
explain.body: The Arrhenius definitions require water as the solvent. Brønsted–Lowry uses proton transfer, so the reaction may take place in the gas phase or in the presence of any solvent. A substance does not need to contain OH⁻ to behave as a Brønsted–Lowry base.

explain.title: Conjugate acid and conjugate base
explain.body: When an acid gives away H⁺, the species left is its conjugate base. When a base receives H⁺, the product is its conjugate acid. In HCl + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻, H₃O⁺ is the conjugate acid and Cl⁻ is the conjugate base.

explain.title: Water can do either job
explain.body: Water accepts H⁺ from HCl, so it acts as a base in that reaction. Water donates H⁺ to NH₃, so it acts as an acid there. A compound that can behave as both an acid and a base is called amphoteric.

mistakes: Do not label an acid or base just by looking for OH⁻; follow the proton transfer.
Do not call the proton acceptor an acid: accepting H⁺ makes it a base.
Do not assume water must be involved in every Brønsted–Lowry acid–base reaction.
Do not confuse a conjugate acid with a conjugate base: accepting H⁺ forms the conjugate acid, while donating H⁺ forms the conjugate base.
When describing water, include both behaviours and the term amphoteric.
